n: Saul is still breathing threats and murder against the Lord’s disciples. He goes to the high priest to extend his campaign. Luke paints him as the Church’s fiercest enemy — making what follows all the more remarkable.
He requests letters to the synagogues in Damascus authorizing him to arrest any followers of “the Way,” men or women, and bring them to Jerusalem in chains.

f.g: A major city in Syria, about 135 miles (220 km) north of Jerusalem, with a large Jewish community.
“The Way” was an early name for the Christian movement.

n: As he nears Damascus, a light from heaven suddenly flashes around him — brighter than the noonday sun, as Paul later recalls.
He falls to the ground and hears a voice: “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” To persecute Christ’s disciples is to persecute Christ himself.

f.g: Doubling a name signals divine urgency and tenderness.

n: “Who are you, Lord?” Saul asks. “I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting.” Saul learns the one he thought was dead is the living Lord. Jesus adds that Saul is only hurting himself by fighting against God.

f.w: it is hard for thee to kick against the pricks
f.g: pricks = goads, pointed sticks used to drive oxen. An ox that kicks against the goad only wounds itself.

n: Trembling and stunned, Saul asks what the Lord wants him to do. He is told to go into the city, where he’ll be instructed. His question marks a total surrender.

f.w: Lord, what wilt thou have me to do?

n: His traveling companions stand speechless; they hear the sound but see no one. Paul’s later account says they saw the light but didn’t understand the voice — the JST of this verse reconciles the two.

f.w: hearing a voice, but seeing no man
f.g: The JST reads: “they saw indeed the light, and were afraid; but they heard not the voice of him that spake to him.”

n: Saul gets up, but when he opens his eyes he can’t see. His companions lead him by the hand into Damascus — the hunter now helpless.

f.g: Physical blindness mirrors the spiritual blindness that is about to be healed.

n: For three days he is blind and neither eats nor drinks — a time of fasting, reflection, and repentance.
In Damascus lives a disciple named Ananias. The Lord calls him in a vision, and he answers, “Here I am, Lord.”

f.g: Paul later describes him as devout and respected by the Jews of Damascus. Not the Ananias of Acts 5.

n: The Lord tells him to go to Straight Street, to the house of Judas, and ask for Saul of Tarsus, who is praying.

f.w: the street which is called Straight
f.g: A main east–west street in Damascus that still exists today.
A prosperous city in Cilicia, known for learning.
The persecutor is now on his knees.

n: Saul has seen in a vision a man named Ananias coming to lay hands on him to restore his sight. God prepares both people at once.
Ananias protests: he has heard from many people about the harm this man did to the saints in Jerusalem.

f.g: “Saints” — holy ones — is a common New Testament name for Church members.

n: And he has come here with authority from the chief priests to arrest everyone who calls on Jesus’s name.

f.w: all that call on thy name

n: The Lord insists: go, for Saul is my chosen instrument to carry my name to Gentiles, kings, and the people of Israel.

f.g: vessel = instrument, tool.

n: The Lord will show him how much he must suffer for his name. Discipleship and sacrifice go together.

f.w: how great things he must suffer for my name's sake

n: Ananias goes, lays his hands on Saul, and calls him “Brother Saul.” He explains that Jesus sent him so Saul can see again and be filled with the Holy Ghost. Faith overcomes fear.

f.g: Ananias welcomes his former enemy as family.

n: Instantly something like scales falls from Saul’s eyes, and he can see. He gets up and is baptized.
After eating, he regains strength and spends some days with the disciples in Damascus — the very people he came to arrest.

f.g: meat = food.

n: Immediately he begins preaching in the synagogues that Jesus is the Son of God.

f.g: straightway = immediately.

f.w: that he is the Son of God

n: Everyone is astonished: isn’t this the man who devastated believers in Jerusalem and came here to arrest them?

f.w: Is not this he that destroyed them

n: Saul grows ever stronger and baffles the Jews of Damascus with proof that Jesus is the Messiah.

f.g: confounded = bewildered, unable to answer.
Literally “putting together” — comparing scriptures to show their fulfillment.

n: After many days, some Jewish leaders plot to kill him. Paul’s letters indicate this period included time in Arabia and lasted about three years.
Saul learns of the plot. They watch the city gates day and night to kill him.

f.g: laying await = lying in ambush.
Paul says the governor under King Aretas also guarded the city.

n: His disciples lower him at night through an opening in the wall in a large basket. The proud persecutor escapes in a humbling way.

f.w: let him down by the wall in a basket

n: In Jerusalem Saul tries to join the disciples, but they are afraid and don’t believe he’s truly a disciple. Trust takes time to rebuild.

f.g: assayed = attempted, tried.

f.w: they were all afraid of him

n: Barnabas — the “son of encouragement” — takes him to the apostles and vouches for him, telling how Saul saw the Lord and preached boldly in Damascus.
Saul moves freely among them in Jerusalem.

f.g: A Hebrew idiom for living and working freely among people.

n: He speaks boldly in Jesus’s name and debates with the Greek-speaking Jews — the same group that opposed Stephen. Now they try to kill him too.

f.g: Hellenistic, Greek-speaking Jews.

n: When the believers learn of this, they take him down to Caesarea and send him home to Tarsus, where he will stay for some years.
The churches throughout Judea, Galilee, and Samaria enjoy a time of peace. Strengthened, living in reverence for the Lord and the comfort of the Holy Ghost, they grow in number.

f.g: Some manuscripts read “the church” — one Church in many places.
edified = built up, strengthened.

f.w: the comfort of the Holy Ghost

n: Luke turns back to Peter, who travels among the congregations and visits the saints at Lydda.

f.g: A town about 25 miles northwest of Jerusalem, on the way to the coast (modern Lod).

n: There he finds a man named Aeneas, paralyzed and bedridden for eight years.

f.g: palsy = paralysis.

n: Peter tells him, “Aeneas, Jesus Christ heals you. Get up and make your bed.” He gets up at once. Peter makes clear the healer is Jesus.
Everyone in Lydda and the plain of Sharon sees him and turns to the Lord.

f.g: The plain of Sharon, the fertile coastal plain.

n: In the port city of Joppa lives a disciple named Tabitha (Greek, Dorcas — both mean “gazelle”). She is known for her constant good deeds and generosity to the poor.

f.g: Modern Jaffa, part of Tel Aviv — the port from which Jonah once fled.

f.w: full of good works and almsdeeds

n: She falls ill and dies. They wash her body and lay it in an upstairs room.

f.g: Washing the body was a customary preparation for burial.

n: Since Lydda is near Joppa, the disciples send two men to Peter, urging him to come without delay.

f.g: nigh = near; about 10–12 miles.

n: Peter goes with them. In the upper room widows stand around weeping, showing him the tunics and garments Dorcas had made for them. Her service is her best eulogy.

f.w: shewing the coats and garments which Dorcas made

n: Peter sends everyone out, kneels and prays, then turns to the body and says, “Tabitha, arise.” She opens her eyes, sees Peter, and sits up — much as Jesus did with Jairus’s daughter.

f.g: Very close to Jesus’s words “Talitha cumi” (“little girl, arise”) in Mark 5:41.

n: He gives her his hand, helps her up, and calls the saints and widows to present her alive.
News spreads through Joppa, and many believe in the Lord.

Peter stays many days in Joppa with a tanner named Simon. Tanners handled dead animals and were considered ritually unclean by strict Jews — a quiet sign that Peter’s boundaries are already loosening before chapter 10.

f.g: tarried = stayed.
